CustomerSegment.name: CustomerSegment
CustomerSegment.doc:
A defined group of customers with shared needs,
behaviours, and willingness to pay. Each segment
has distinct needs and may require distinct value
propositions.

userFacing.shortDescription: A defined group of customers with shared needs and willingness to pay.

purposiveDescription.description: A group of people your service is designed for — people who share similar needs and reasons for choosing you. When you define your customer segments, the system uses them to connect your value propositions, pricing, and channels to the right audiences.

weightedRelationships.rationale: Each segment has one or more propositions designed for it. A change to the target segment requires reassessing the value promises made to it.
Offerings are what the segment actually receives. A change to the target audience requires reassessing what is offered to them.
Channels are how segments are reached. A change to the target segment may require reviewing acquisition and delivery channels, but the relationship is many-to-many.

ValueProposition.name: ValueProposition
ValueProposition.doc:
A specific promise of value to a specific customer
segment. Defines what the customer gets, how it
differs from alternatives, and why it matters.

userFacing.shortDescription: A promise of value to a customer segment — what they get and why it matters.

purposiveDescription.description: The core promise your service makes to a particular group of customers — what they get from you and why they'd choose you over the alternatives. When you define a value proposition, the system holds it as the anchor that your activities, resources, and pricing all exist to deliver.

weightedRelationships.rationale: The offering is the concrete realisation of the proposition. A change to the value promise requires reassessing what is offered to deliver it.
Every value proposition is made to a specific segment. A change to the promise of value requires reassessing the audience it addresses.
Claims articulate how the proposition differs from alternatives. A change to the proposition may require reviewing its supporting claims, but a proposition can exist before claims are formalised.

ServiceOffering.name: ServiceOffering
ServiceOffering.doc:
A packaged, deliverable unit of service that realises
one or more value propositions for one or more
segments. This is the unit at which pricing, resource
requirements, and pathway mapping are defined

userFacing.shortDescription: A packaged unit of service that can be priced, resourced, and delivered to customers.

purposiveDescription.description: A distinct service that your business offers — something a customer can choose, pay for, and receive. When you define a service offering, the system connects it to the activities required to deliver it, the resources it consumes, and the price the customer pays.

weightedRelationships.rationale: A service offering is the concrete realisation of a value proposition. A change to what is offered requires reassessing the promise of value it delivers.
Every service offering exists for defined customer segments. A change to what is offered requires reassessing who it is for.
Each offering has a pricing basis. A change to the offering directly affects how it is priced.
Every service offering requires activities to deliver it. A change to the offering requires reassessing the activity types involved.
Channels deliver service offerings to customers. A change to the offering may require reviewing delivery channels, but the coupling is not definitional.
The catalogue records the business decision to offer something. A change to the offering may require updating catalogue entries, but the catalogue is operational, not definitional.
Claims support the value proposition which the offering delivers. A change to the offering may require reviewing claims, but the link is mediated through the value proposition.

Resources are consumed by activities which deliver offerings. A change to the offering may affect resource requirements, but the relationship is indirect — mediated through activity types and capabilities.

Channel.name: Channel
Channel.doc:
A means by which customers discover, access, and
interact with the service. Channels have reach,
cost, and conversion characteristics.

userFacing.shortDescription: A way that customers find, reach, or receive your service.

purposiveDescription.description: A way that customers find you, reach you, or receive your service — your website, a referral network, a walk-in counter, an app. When you define your channels, the system tracks which customer segments each channel serves and how your service offerings are delivered through them.

weightedRelationships.rationale: Channels serve customer segments. A change to a channel may require reviewing which segments it reaches, but the coupling is operational and many-to-many.
Channels deliver service offerings. A change to a channel may require reviewing which offerings flow through it, but the coupling is loose.

DifferentiationClaim.name: DifferentiationClaim
DifferentiationClaim.doc:
An explicit statement of how this service differs
from available alternatives, from the customer's
perspective. Each claim should be testable.

userFacing.shortDescription: An explicit, testable statement of how your service differs from alternatives.

purposiveDescription.description: An explicit statement of how your service differs from the alternatives, from the customer's perspective. Each claim should be testable — something you can back up with evidence. When you define differentiation claims, the system records them as commitments your service is designed to fulfil.

weightedRelationships.rationale: Claims exist to substantiate a value proposition. A change to a claim requires reassessing the proposition it supports — a claim without a proposition is orphaned.
Claims relate to offerings indirectly, via the value proposition. A change to a claim has a distant effect on offerings — mediated through the proposition.

ServiceSubject.name: ServiceSubject
ServiceSubject.doc:
The entity upon which a service is performed. The dog
being groomed, the patient receiving care, the garment
being laundered, the item being repaired.
A service subject is structurally distinct from a

userFacing.shortDescription: The entity upon which a service is performed — a person, animal, object, or organisation that receives the service.

purposiveDescription.description: The thing your service acts on — the dog being groomed, the patient receiving care, the garment being cleaned, the item being repaired. A service subject may have needs independent of whoever commissioned the service, and governance obligations may attach to the subject directly. When you identify your service subjects, the system tracks what is being served, in what condition, and with what independent requirements — separately from who is paying or making decisions.

weightedRelationships.rationale: What is offered depends directly on the nature of the subject. A different breed, clinical condition, or item type requires reassessing the offering.
Governance obligations attach to the subject independently of the customer. Duty of care is to the dog, the patient, the object in custody.
The subject's characteristics directly determine the activities required — breed-specific grooming, patient-specific procedures, item-specific repair.
Subject and participants are related — participants commission, fund, or authorise services on or for the subject — but they are independently defined.
Different customer segments may involve different subject types, but the segment is defined by its needs and willingness to pay, not by the subject.

ServiceParticipant.name: ServiceParticipant
ServiceParticipant.doc:
An entity involved in a service engagement in a
defined role. The person who pays, the organisation
that commissions, the carer who makes decisions,
the expert called in for assessment.
A service part

userFacing.shortDescription: An entity involved in a service engagement in a defined role — customer, payer, commissioner, decision-maker, or any other role.

purposiveDescription.description: Any person or organisation involved in a service engagement in a defined role. The person who pays, the organisation that commissions, the carer who makes decisions, the expert called in for assessment — any entity with influence on how the service proceeds. When you identify your service participants, the system tracks who is involved, in what capacity, and how their status affects the service workflow. The set of possible roles is open — the model does not constrain what kinds of participation your service may involve.

weightedRelationships.rationale: The participant's role is defined in relation to the subject — they commission, fund, authorise, or contribute to the service on or for the subject.
The participant influences the offering — a commissioner may constrain scope, a payer may limit options — but the offering is primarily shaped by the subject's needs.
Participants often belong to or represent a customer segment, but the mapping is characterising — a segment is not defined by its participants.
Governance requirements may apply to participants (commissioner must approve, payer must authorise), but the primary governance binding is to the subject.

CatalogueEntry.name: CatalogueEntry
CatalogueEntry.doc:
The business decision to offer an item for sale or
use within a service. References an item definition
and adds business-context properties.
The four-layer model separates what something
intrinsically

userFacing.shortDescription: A record of something your business has decided to offer, with its price and status.

purposiveDescription.description: A record of something your business has decided to offer — whether that's a menu item, a treatment, a course, or any other unit you sell or provide. The catalogue entry connects what the thing intrinsically is to how your business offers it: its price, availability, and status. When you add a catalogue entry, the system tracks it as part of your active offering.

weightedRelationships.rationale: The catalogue records what is offered. A change to a catalogue entry may require reviewing the offering it represents, but the catalogue is the operational wrapper, not the strategic definition.
Catalogue entries link to external knowledge sources. A change to a catalogue entry may require reviewing its external references — the four-layer item model connects them.
Inventory tracks stock of catalogue items. A change to a catalogue entry may require updating its associated inventory records.

ExternalReference.name: ExternalReference
ExternalReference.doc:
A link to knowledge that lives outside the system.
The system does not own this data; it points to it.
Business meta model concept. Domain-agnostic:
  Coffee shop: supplier datasheet, origin cert
  He

userFacing.shortDescription: A link to authoritative knowledge that lives outside your system.

purposiveDescription.description: A link to knowledge that lives outside your system — a supplier datasheet, a regulatory standard, a clinical guideline, an accreditation body. The system doesn't own this information; it points to it, so you always know where authoritative external knowledge sits in relation to your service.

weightedRelationships.rationale: External references attach to catalogue items. A change to an external reference may require reviewing the catalogue entries that depend on it.

ActivityType.name: ActivityType
ActivityType.doc:
A defined type of activity within the business.
Every activity has a type, and every type belongs
to one of the five taxonomy categories.

userFacing.shortDescription: A defined kind of business activity, classified into one of five categories.

purposiveDescription.description: Something your business does — an identifiable unit of work that the system holds, tracks, and uses. In this system, every activity is an activity of one of the following types: service delivery, enabling, governance, development, or overhead. When you assign one of these types to an activity, the system will use that information to plan resources, allocate costs, and verify that governance requirements are being met for each kind of work.

weightedRelationships.rationale: Cost allocation is structurally determined by activity type — every cost line traces back to an activity category.
Granularity level directly governs how an activity type is tracked and costed — envelope vs category vs tracked.
Budgets aggregate by activity type but the relationship is indirect — mediated through cost allocation.
Activity records are typed by activity type but the record is an operational artefact, not a structural dependency.
Resources are consumed by activities but the mapping is many-to-many and context-dependent.
Channels deliver services which contain activities, but the relationship is distant — mediated through service offerings.

ActivityRecord.name: ActivityRecord
ActivityRecord.doc:
A recorded instance of an activity. At the tracked
level, the system produces these for every observable
activity. At coarser levels, they are estimated
aggregates.

userFacing.shortDescription: A recorded instance of an activity that actually happened.

purposiveDescription.description: A recorded instance of an activity that actually happened — the system's record that a specific piece of work was done, by whom, for how long, and using what resources. At the most detailed tracking level, the system creates one of these for every observable activity. At coarser levels, they are estimated aggregates.

weightedRelationships.rationale: Every record is typed by an activity type. If the record format or granularity changes, the activity type may need reviewing — but an operational change to how records are produced does not redefine what the activity type is.

ActivityBudget.name: ActivityBudget
ActivityBudget.doc:
A planned allocation of activity volume by type,
period, and resource. The activity-level equivalent
of a financial budget.

userFacing.shortDescription: A planned allocation of activity volume by type and period.

purposiveDescription.description: A planned allocation of how much activity of each type your business expects in a given period — the activity-level equivalent of a financial budget. When you define an activity budget, the system can compare what actually happened against what was planned, and surface gaps.

weightedRelationships.rationale: Budgets are structured by activity type. If the budget changes (e.g. planned volumes revised), the activity type may need reviewing — but a quantitative change to volume does not redefine what the activity type is.
Activity budgets feed into financial projections as volume inputs. If the budget changes, the projection may need updating — but the projection aggregates many inputs beyond activity volumes.

ActivityGranularity.name: ActivityGranularity
ActivityGranularity.doc:
Policy declaration: the granularity level at which
activity is tracked for a given business area.

userFacing.shortDescription: A policy declaration of how precisely activity is tracked in a given area.

purposiveDescription.description: A policy declaration: how precisely does your business track activity in a given area? The system supports three levels — envelope (a rough total), category (broken down by type), and tracked (every individual activity recorded). Different parts of your business can operate at different levels at the same time, and you can refine the level as your needs evolve.

weightedRelationships.rationale: Granularity governs how activity types are tracked. If the granularity policy changes, the activity types in that area may need reviewing — but a policy change about tracking precision does not redefine what the activity type is.

Granularity determines the detail level of records. If the granularity changes, the record format may need adjustment — but records are produced by the tracking system, not directly defined by the policy declaration.

ActivityCostAllocation.name: ActivityCostAllocation
ActivityCostAllocation.doc:
The mapping from an activity (or aggregate) to its
financial cost. Makes resource consumption visible
to the financial model.

userFacing.shortDescription: The mapping from an activity type to its financial cost.

purposiveDescription.description: The mapping from an activity to its financial cost — how much does it cost each time this kind of work is done? When you define cost allocations, the system can connect your activity model to your financial model, making resource consumption visible in financial terms.

weightedRelationships.rationale: Cost allocations are defined per activity type. If the allocation changes (method, estimated cost), the activity type may need reviewing — but a financial change to how the activity is costed does not redefine what the activity type is.

Cost allocations use cost driver rates to compute per-activity costs. If the allocation method changes, the cost driver may need reviewing — but the driver describes the resource's cost behaviour independently of how individual activities are costed against it.
Cost allocations ultimately feed unit economics through cost drivers. If an allocation changes, unit economics may need updating — but the relationship is mediated through cost drivers, not direct.

ResourceType.name: ResourceType
ResourceType.doc:
A category of resource required to operate the
service delivery system. Each type has acquisition
characteristics, capacity constraints, and cost
profiles.

userFacing.shortDescription: A category of resource needed to run the service — people, equipment, premises, or external services.

purposiveDescription.description: A kind of thing your business needs in order to operate — staff, equipment, premises, technology, or external services such as a laboratory or a contractor. The system holds each resource type as a tracked concept. When you define your resource types, the system uses them to plan capacity, understand your cost base, and identify where you might be constrained.

weightedRelationships.rationale: Instances are typed by ResourceType. If the type definition changes (category, cost profile, capacity unit), every instance of that type needs reassessment.

Constraints are scoped to specific resource types. If the resource type changes, the constraints that limit its availability need reassessment — a constraint on a specific resource assumes specific properties of that type.

Capabilities combine resources into service functions. A change to a resource type may require reviewing the capabilities that use it, but capabilities are resilient to substitution within a resource category.

Capacity models describe throughput given a resource configuration. A change to a resource type may affect throughput calculations, but the relationship is mediated through the specific configuration.
Cost drivers are linked to resources. A change to a resource type (especially its cost profile) may require reviewing the associated cost driver, but the link is structural rather than definitional.
Activities consume resources. A change to a resource type may affect which activities can be performed, but the coupling is many-to-many and context-dependent.

ResourceInstance.name: ResourceInstance
ResourceInstance.doc:
A specific resource available to the business at
a defined capacity and cost. Represents planning-
level archetypes ("a prescribing clinician at
0.5 FTE") rather than named individuals.

userFacing.shortDescription: A specific resource available at a defined capacity and cost.

purposiveDescription.description: A specific resource available to your business at a defined capacity and cost — not a named individual, but a planning-level description like 'a prescribing clinician at 0.5 FTE' or 'one licensed copy of the booking system'. When you define resource instances, the system uses them to model your actual operating capacity.

weightedRelationships.rationale: An instance is a concrete realisation of its type. If the instance changes (capacity, cost, availability), the type may need reviewing — but an operational change to one instance does not redefine the resource type's category, acquisition method, or capacity unit.

Capacity models are built from resource configurations. A change to an instance (e.g. clinician drops from 0.8 to 0.5 FTE) may require reviewing the throughput calculation, but the capacity model aggregates across instances.

Capability.name: Capability
Capability.doc:
An organised combination of resources that produces
a defined service function. Capabilities bridge the
gap between raw resources and service delivery — you
don't deliver care with "a doctor" and "a s

userFacing.shortDescription: An organised combination of resources that produces a defined service function.

purposiveDescription.description: An organised combination of resources that together produce a defined service function — like 'the ability to conduct a monitoring review' (which requires a clinician, a lab interface, and a clinical record system). You don't deliver services with individual resources; you deliver them with capabilities. When you define capabilities, the system connects your resources to the service offerings they enable.

weightedRelationships.rationale: Capabilities enable service offerings. If a capability changes, the offerings it enables need reassessment — you can't offer what you can't deliver.
Capabilities are defined by the resources they combine. If a capability changes (e.g. a new resource requirement is added), the resource types involved need reassessment.

Capabilities are the downstream end of strategy-to-operations traceability. If a capability changes, the mapping from strategic objectives to that capability may need reviewing, but the mapping is a declared connection, not a definitional dependency.
Capacity models describe throughput for a resource configuration that delivers a capability. If the capability changes, the throughput model may need recalibrating, but the relationship is indirect.

CapacityModel.name: CapacityModel
CapacityModel.doc:

userFacing.shortDescription: The relationship between your resource configuration and service throughput.

purposiveDescription.description: The relationship between your resource configuration and how much service you can deliver — for example, 'with one clinician at 0.5 FTE, we can support 20 active patients.' This is a planning assertion that the system holds, not a computed formula. When you define a capacity model, the system knows your throughput limits and can surface when you're approaching them.

weightedRelationships.rationale: A capacity model makes claims about throughput given a resource configuration. If the capacity model changes, the resource types it references may need reassessment — but the resource type exists independently of any one capacity model.

Capacity models and constraints are complementary planning concepts. If the capacity model changes (e.g. higher throughput targets), the constraints that limit resource availability may need reviewing.

userFacing.shortDescription: A limit on resource availability that affects service delivery.

purposiveDescription.description: A limit on the availability or use of a resource that affects your ability to deliver services — regulatory, financial, temporal, or contractual. When you define resource constraints, the system tracks them alongside your resources so that capacity planning reflects real-world limits, not just theoretical availability.

weightedRelationships.rationale: Constraints are defined against specific resource types. If a constraint changes (e.g. a regulatory limit is tightened or lifted), the resource type it governs needs reassessment — the type's effective availability and cost profile may have changed.
Constraints limit what a resource configuration can deliver. If a constraint changes, the throughput assumptions in the capacity model may need reviewing.

purposiveDescription.description: A point-in-time record of how much stock you have of something in your catalogue — how many tablets, how many bags of coffee beans, how many bottles of cleaning product. This is operational tracking: it tells the system what you have right now, so it can flag when you're running low. Distinct from resource planning, which is about strategic capacity.

weightedRelationships.rationale: Inventory tracks stock of catalogue items. If the inventory record changes (e.g. stock level drops below threshold), the catalogue entry's availability status needs reassessment — the catalogue promises what inventory must deliver.

purposiveDescription.description: A declared connection between a strategic objective and the capabilities that contribute to achieving it. When you map objectives to capabilities, the system can trace from 'what are we trying to achieve?' down to 'what resources and service functions make that possible?' — closing the loop between strategy and operations.

weightedRelationships.rationale: The mapping declares which capabilities support a strategic objective. If the mapping changes, the capabilities involved need reassessment — they may gain or lose strategic justification.

RevenueStream.name: RevenueStream
RevenueStream.doc: A mechanism by which income is generated.

userFacing.shortDescription: A mechanism by which the business generates income from its services.

purposiveDescription.description: A way your business earns money — each revenue stream connects a customer segment, a triggering event (like completing an assessment or renewing a subscription), and a pricing model. When you define your revenue streams, the system can project income and connect it to the services that generate it.

weightedRelationships.rationale: Each revenue stream references a pricing model. If the revenue stream changes (e.g. new trigger event, different source segment), the pricing model may need reassessment to match.
Financial projections aggregate revenue streams. If a revenue stream changes, the projection that depends on it needs reassessment.
Revenue streams inform the revenue side of unit economics. If a stream changes, revenue-per-unit may need reviewing — but unit economics are per-offering, not per-stream.

CostDriver.name: CostDriver
CostDriver.doc: A structural factor that generates cost.

userFacing.shortDescription: A structural factor that generates cost in the business — linked to a resource or activity.

purposiveDescription.description: A structural factor that generates cost in your business — something that, as it scales or recurs, drives your expenditure. Each cost driver is linked to a resource or an activity. When you define your cost drivers, the system connects your cost structure to the resources and activities that produce it, so you can see where money goes and why.

weightedRelationships.rationale: Cost drivers characterise resources financially. If a cost driver changes (e.g. unit cost revised), the resource type's cost profile may need updating — but the resource type's category, acquisition method, and structural definition are independent of its cost behaviour.
Unit economics aggregate costs per service unit. If a cost driver changes, the cost-per-unit calculation needs reassessment — cost drivers are the input to that calculation.
Cost allocations map activities to costs. If a cost driver changes, the allocation method may need reviewing — but the allocation is a mapping mechanism, not directly defined by the cost driver.

Revenue streams and cost drivers together determine profitability. If a cost driver changes significantly, revenue assumptions may need reviewing — but the relationship is indirect, mediated through unit economics and financial projections.

UnitEconomics.name: UnitEconomics
UnitEconomics.doc: The financial profile of a single unit of service delivery.

userFacing.shortDescription: The revenue, cost, and margin for a single unit of service delivery.

purposiveDescription.description: The financial profile of delivering one unit of a service — what you earn, what it costs, and the margin between them. When you define unit economics for each service offering, the system can assess whether individual services are financially viable and how changes to pricing or costs would affect the picture.

weightedRelationships.rationale: Unit economics characterise an offering's financial viability. If the unit economics change (e.g. margin drops below zero), the offering itself needs reassessment — but the offering's definition doesn't depend on its economics.
Financial projections aggregate unit-level economics. If unit economics change, the projection may need updating — but the projection also depends on volume assumptions and other inputs.

PricingModel.name: PricingModel
PricingModel.doc: The logic that determines what a customer pays.

userFacing.shortDescription: How prices are set for services — per-episode, subscription, tiered, or other basis.

purposiveDescription.description: The logic that determines what a customer pays for a service — per-episode, subscription, tiered, sliding scale, or flat fee. When you define a pricing model, the system applies it to the relevant service offerings and uses it in revenue projections and unit economics calculations.

weightedRelationships.rationale: Revenue streams reference a pricing model as their revenue mechanism. If the pricing model changes, the revenue projections that depend on it need reassessment.

Pricing models define how offerings are charged for. If the pricing logic changes, the offering's commercial packaging may need reviewing — but the offering itself (what is delivered, to whom, using what resources) is defined independently of how it is priced.

Unit economics calculate margin per unit of service. If the pricing model changes, the revenue-per-unit figure needs reviewing — but unit economics also depend on cost factors that are independent of pricing.

userFacing.shortDescription: A forward-looking financial picture combining revenues, costs, and growth assumptions.

purposiveDescription.description: A named projection of your business's financial future over a defined period — combining your revenue streams, cost drivers, and growth assumptions into a forward-looking picture. When you define a financial projection, the system links it to a scenario so you can compare different versions of the future side by side.

weightedRelationships.rationale: A projection aggregates revenue streams. If the projection changes (e.g. revised timeline, different scenario), the revenue streams feeding it may need reviewing — but revenue streams exist independently of any one projection.
A projection aggregates cost drivers. If the projection changes, the cost assumptions may need reviewing — but cost drivers exist independently of any one projection.

purposiveDescription.description: A regulatory, legal, or standards obligation that your business must satisfy — and the system tracks it as a concrete, testable commitment, not just a policy statement. Each governance requirement is connected to the evidence that demonstrates compliance and, where formalised, to the constraint rules that the system can check. When you define governance requirements, the system builds a traceability chain from obligation through to proof.

weightedRelationships.rationale: Each governance requirement defines what evidence must be produced. If the requirement changes, the evidence records need reassessment — you may need different proof, different frequency, or different responsible roles.

Governance requirements often impose resource constraints (regulatory qualification requirements, capacity limits). If a requirement changes, associated resource constraints may need reviewing — but not all requirements produce resource constraints.
A change to a governance requirement may require reviewing the relationship through which it is enforced, but the relationship exists independently of any single requirement (H1, H5).

When you define audit evidence records, the system knows what proof exists and can surface gaps where evidence is missing or overdue.

Each relationship has a defined nature, mutual obligations, and a health profile. When you define stakeholder relationships, the system tracks who you interact with, what you owe each other, and whether the relationship is working well.

When you define cooperative arrangements, the system tracks what is jointly produced, how responsibility is divided, and how the arrangement's effectiveness is assessed.

weightedRelationships.rationale: A cooperative arrangement defines shared activities. A change to the arrangement directly affects what activities are performed and by whom (H1).
Some cooperative arrangements define jointly-delivered services. A change to the arrangement may fundamentally alter what can be offered (H1).
Cooperative arrangements may involve shared resources, but the resource types exist independently (H4).

When you define external dependencies, the system tracks what you depend on, how critical each dependency is, what contingency plans exist, and what risks threaten continuity of supply.

Community relationships are constitutive of your identity, not transactional. When you define community relationships, the system tracks how communities shape your service and how you engage with them.

A change to the regulatory relationship (e.g. new regulator, changed inspection regime) directly affects what governance requirements apply. Definitional for regulatory-natured relationships (H1).

A change to a stakeholder relationship may affect what services can be offered (e.g. loss of a commissioning relationship), but the offering's identity is defined independently in ServiceConcept (H1, H4).

A cooperative arrangement defines shared activities. A change to the arrangement directly affects what activities are performed and by whom (H1).

Dependencies have cost implications (supplier pricing, contractual terms), but cost drivers are characterising, not definitional (H1, H2).
Community relationships shape what the business offers (community needs influence service design), but the link is characterising, not definitional (H1).
Communities overlap with customer segments, but they are not the same thing — a community relationship may serve non-customers (H4).
Participation patterns are defined for specific service offerings — the ref relationship is typed. A change to how customers participate directly affects the offering's delivery model (H1).
Participation generates activities (self-service actions, shared decision-making), but the activity types exist independently (H4).
Participation mode may affect which channels are used (e.g. self-service requires a digital channel), but channels serve multiple purposes (H4).

architecturalSections.name: bfo
architecturalSections.purposiveDescription: The shared foundation spanning both stacks. BFO is an ISO standard upper ontology providing the categorical framework — Continuant, Occurrent, Role, Disposition, Quality, Function — that classifies everything in the architecture. Every entity in every layer traces upward to a BFO category. BFO determines valid reasoning patterns: what can bear a Role, what can participate in a Process, what is a Quality of what.
architecturalSections.shortDescription: The shared upper ontology spanning both stacks, providing the categorical framework for everything in the architecture.
architecturalSections.representationalModalitySummary: OWL 2 DL. Imported directly from the OBO Foundry as a maintained external ontology.
architecturalSections.persistenceSummary: Target: triple store (knowledge graph). Currently: referenced in discussion papers and architecture diagram; not yet implemented.
architecturalSections.interfacesSummary: Vertical downward to both domain ontologies (left stack) and system ontological categories (right stack). Spans both stacks as a shared foundation; does not connect horizontally.
architecturalSections.domainIllustrationSummary: For Paws: Sam is a BFO Continuant bearing a Role; a ServiceOffering is an Occurrent; a Room is an Independent Continuant; a PricingRule is a Generically Dependent Continuant.

architecturalSections.name: domain-ontologies
architecturalSections.purposiveDescription: Mid-level BFO-aligned ontologies providing domain-specific semantic grounding between BFO's abstract categories and the BMM's structural vocabulary. The selection of domain ontologies during tenant onboarding gives each tenant its semantic character — healthcare tenants use OGMS and GSSO; commercial tenants use OCE. All use IAO for information entities.
architecturalSections.shortDescription: Mid-level BFO-aligned ontologies providing tenant-specific semantic grounding between BFO and the BMM vocabulary.
architecturalSections.representationalModalitySummary: OWL 2 DL. Existing OBO Foundry ontologies, imported directly.
architecturalSections.persistenceSummary: Target: triple store (knowledge graph), alongside BFO. Currently: referenced only.
architecturalSections.interfacesSummary: Vertical downward to BMM General vocabulary. Vertical upward to BFO. Horizontal rightward to system ontological categories — the topmost horizontal mapping.
architecturalSections.domainIllustrationSummary: For Paws: OCE (Ontology of Commercial Enterprises) as primary domain ontology. For GSL: OGMS+GSSO+IAO — same BMM structure, fundamentally different semantic grounding.

architecturalSections.name: bmm-general-vocabulary
architecturalSections.purposiveDescription: The classification engine for the business side. 34 part defs across six concerns defining the structural templates for what a service business is. Raw business information is mapped to these templates. The BMM General vocabulary is domain-neutral — the same part defs apply to a dog grooming salon, a coffee shop, and a gender identity clinic. This is the level at which cross-domain validation operates.
architecturalSections.shortDescription: The 34 domain-neutral structural templates defining what a service business is, across six concerns.
architecturalSections.representationalModalitySummary: SysML v2 part defs. The most mature section — 34 part defs with full comprehension metadata (34/34 UserFacing, PurposiveDescription, Comprehension; 96 WeightedRelationship).
architecturalSections.persistenceSummary: Currently: .sysml files in the git repository. Target: knowledge graph (canonical) with SysML v2 files as projection.
architecturalSections.interfacesSummary: Vertical downward: instantiated by the business instance layer. Vertical upward: traces through domain ontologies to BFO. Horizontal rightward: many-to-many mapping to BSMM General vocabulary.
architecturalSections.domainIllustrationSummary: For Paws: exclusively General vocabulary — 34 part defs provide the structural skeleton for all service offerings, staff, facilities, pricing, and stakeholder relationships.

architecturalSections.name: business-instance
architecturalSections.purposiveDescription: The concrete populated data for a specific tenant. Where the BMM General vocabulary provides structural templates (part defs), the business instance provides the actual content (part usages). Relation binding happens here: entities are stitched together by confirming typed relations. The user has the most agency at this layer — convention-over-configuration narrows the space of valid connections.
architecturalSections.shortDescription: The concrete populated data for a specific tenant — part usages instantiating BMM part defs.
architecturalSections.representationalModalitySummary: SysML v2 part usages instantiating BMM part defs. Per-domain .sysml files in the exercises directory.
architecturalSections.persistenceSummary: Currently: .sysml files. Target: knowledge graph (canonical) — business instance data as OWL individuals.
architecturalSections.interfacesSummary: Vertical downward to operational domains. Vertical upward: every instance is an instantiation of a BMM General concept. Horizontal rightward to system instance — the realised-by relationship.
architecturalSections.domainIllustrationSummary: For Paws: 5 ServiceOfferings, 3 StaffMembers, 6 Rooms, PricingRule matrix, 10 CostCategories, 7 StakeholderModel instantiations, and all typed relations binding them together.

architecturalSections.purposiveDescription: How the business actually operates — in business language, not system language. The Session 73 correction: these are business model content, not system descriptions. They describe how the business operates and inform what systems are needed, but they remain squarely on the business model side. Currently partially implicit — they emerge from walking the relation graph in the instance layer.
architecturalSections.shortDescription: How the business actually operates, in business language — the operational areas that emerge from the business instance.
architecturalSections.representationalModalitySummary: SysML v2. Currently partially implicit — operational domains emerge from the instance layer but are not explicitly modelled as distinct packages.
architecturalSections.persistenceSummary: Currently: implicit in the instance layer structure. Target: explicit in the knowledge graph and/or SysML model.
architecturalSections.interfacesSummary: Vertical downward to business process patterns. Vertical upward: emerges from the business instance. Horizontal rightward to system domains. Inside the green container: operates under rules and constraints.
architecturalSections.domainIllustrationSummary: For Paws: nine operational domains — Booking, Scheduling, Finance, Customer Management, Inventory, Compliance, Reporting, Marketing, and Document Management — each in Sam's language.

architecturalSections.name: business-process-patterns
architecturalSections.purposiveDescription: The most dynamic layer of the left stack. Process patterns operate at three abstraction levels: universal archetypes (Resource Allocation, Scheduling, Fulfilment, etc.), BMM-parameterised patterns, and domain-specific instances. This is the crossing point — business process patterns compile to executable artefacts on the right stack through the process specification layer pipeline.
architecturalSections.shortDescription: Dynamic behaviour and flows at three abstraction levels — archetypes, BMM-parameterised patterns, and domain-specific instances.
architecturalSections.representationalModalitySummary: SysML v2 for archetype and pattern definitions. Process sketch DSL (proposed) for human-readable instances. Currently: described in discussion papers; not yet formally modelled.
architecturalSections.persistenceSummary: Currently: discussion papers only. Target: knowledge graph (canonical) with SysML v2 as projection.
architecturalSections.interfacesSummary: Vertical upward: parameterised by BMM vocabulary. Horizontal rightward: the pipeline crossing — executed as operational simulation workflows. Inside the green container: operates under rules and constraints.
architecturalSections.domainIllustrationSummary: For Paws: Resource Allocation (room to groom), Scheduling (appointment booking), Transaction (payment), Fulfilment (deliver groom), Replenishment (reorder shampoo) — each determined by typed relations in the instance.

architecturalSections.name: system-ontological-categories
architecturalSections.purposiveDescription: The right-stack counterpart of the domain ontologies. Classifies system entities using BFO: a workflow is a Process (Occurrent), a data record is an Information Content Entity (Continuant via IAO), an event is an Occurrent with instantaneous temporal extent, a system state is a Quality. These are not arbitrary labels — they are BFO-typed, enabling ontological consistency checking between system and business entities.
architecturalSections.shortDescription: BFO-typed categories classifying what kinds of things can exist in a business system — the right-stack counterpart of domain ontologies.
architecturalSections.representationalModalitySummary: OWL 2 DL — ontological categories above the formalism boundary. Not yet implemented.
architecturalSections.persistenceSummary: Target: triple store (knowledge graph) as named classes and axioms. Currently: exists only in discussion papers.
architecturalSections.interfacesSummary: Vertical downward: classifies everything in the BSMM General vocabulary. Vertical upward to BFO. Horizontal leftward: mapping to domain ontologies — the topmost horizontal mapping constraining what system entities can realise which business entities.
architecturalSections.domainIllustrationSummary: For Paws: a BookingWorkflow is a Process; a GroomingRecord is an Information Content Entity; a PaymentReceivedEvent is a Process Boundary; a RoomAvailabilityState is a Quality.

architecturalSections.name: bsmm-general-vocabulary
architecturalSections.purposiveDescription: The right-stack counterpart of the BMM General vocabulary. Defines what a business system is — the domain-neutral system concepts any Ontara tenant would need. Organised into six capability groups (B25): Persistence and Data Management, Process Orchestration, Evaluation and Reasoning, Observation and Self-Knowledge, Integration and Communication, Identity and Access. Horizontal mappings to the BMM are many-to-many.
architecturalSections.shortDescription: Domain-neutral system concepts organised into six capability groups — the right-stack counterpart of the BMM vocabulary.
architecturalSections.representationalModalitySummary: SysML v2 part defs. Designed (Session 76 discussion paper) but not yet implemented. Individual concepts exist scattered across Foundation, Knowledge, ServiceDelivery, Platform, and Operations.
architecturalSections.persistenceSummary: Target: knowledge graph (canonical) with SysML v2 as projection. Currently: distributed across existing SysML packages without explicit BSMM organisation.
architecturalSections.interfacesSummary: Vertical downward: instantiated by the system instance. Vertical upward: traces to system ontological categories. Horizontal leftward: explicit many-to-many mappings to BMM General vocabulary.
architecturalSections.domainIllustrationSummary: For Paws: PersistencePolicy for data storage, ProcessSpecification for workflow shapes, ConstraintEvaluationSpec for scheduling rules, ExternalServiceBinding for payment integration, CommunicationChannel for notifications.

architecturalSections.name: system-instance
architecturalSections.purposiveDescription: The right-stack counterpart of the business instance. Where the business instance holds the concrete populated data for a specific tenant, the system instance holds the concrete system configuration: which database, which workflow engine configuration, which integration endpoints, which access control policies. The system instance makes the generic BSMM vocabulary into this tenant's system.
architecturalSections.shortDescription: The concrete system configuration for a specific tenant — which database, workflow engine, integration endpoints, and access control policies.
architecturalSections.representationalModalitySummary: SysML v2 part usages instantiating BSMM part defs. Currently partially implicit in the coffee shop demonstrator — the running application embodies choices not explicitly modelled.
architecturalSections.persistenceSummary: Target: knowledge graph (canonical) with SysML v2 as projection. Currently: embodied in application code and configuration.
architecturalSections.interfacesSummary: Vertical downward to system domains. Vertical upward: every element instantiates a BSMM General concept. Horizontal leftward to business instance — the realised-by relationship.
architecturalSections.domainIllustrationSummary: For Paws: PostgreSQL for transactional data, Temporal for workflows, appointment-based scheduling config, base-price-plus-surcharge pricing engine, payment processor integration, notification templates, role-based access control.

architecturalSections.name: system-domains
architecturalSections.purposiveDescription: The right-stack counterpart of operational domains. Where the left stack's operational domains describe how the business operates in business language, system domains describe the same reality in system language — the running software modules. The model remains connected at runtime: the system does not generate and step aside. The coffee shop demonstrator has system domains as implemented modules.
architecturalSections.shortDescription: The running software modules that realise business operations — the right-stack counterpart of operational domains.
architecturalSections.representationalModalitySummary: SysML v2 for model descriptions; the system domains also have an execution dimension as running code. Dual nature: model content and operational modules.
architecturalSections.persistenceSummary: Dual: model descriptions in SysML v2 / knowledge graph; running instances in their own operational stores (PostgreSQL, workflow state, CDR).
architecturalSections.interfacesSummary: Vertical downward to operational simulation. Vertical upward: instantiates system instance configurations. Horizontal leftward to operational domains — realised-by. Inside the green container: operates under rules and constraints.
architecturalSections.domainIllustrationSummary: For Paws: Booking Service, Grooming Workflow Manager, Financial Module, Customer Management, Inventory Tracker, Compliance Module — each mapping horizontally to a business operational domain.

architecturalSections.name: operational-simulation
architecturalSections.purposiveDescription: The BSMM made operational: Temporal workflows coordinating business execution per tenant, with human actors and connected applications as participants. This is where business operations happen in system terms. The groomer, the receptionist, the payment processor are all participants inside the simulation. Every workflow, activity, and state transition traces through BSMM to BMM to ontology to BFO, preserving semantic lineage end-to-end.
architecturalSections.shortDescription: The bottom of the right stack — where the business system is live, with Temporal workflows coordinating execution per tenant.
architecturalSections.representationalModalitySummary: Temporal workflows, event streams, and durable state management — execution formalisms generated from the SysML model (A3). The coffee shop FulfilDrink workflow is a working example.
architecturalSections.persistenceSummary: Temporal workflow state (durable, resumable), event logs, and operational databases. The simulation state is the business's current operational state — the most ephemeral section, changing continuously.
architecturalSections.interfacesSummary: Upward from system domains. Cross-cutting: the reflective simulation reads continuously. Inside the green container: rules and constraints govern permissible behaviour. Horizontal leftward to business process patterns — the pipeline crossing.
architecturalSections.domainIllustrationSummary: For Paws: the living business — a StandardGroom workflow assigns groomer Pol to a Medium Labrador, moves through bath/dry/style stages, calculates price with surcharges, and processes payment, all with full semantic lineage.

architecturalSections.name: reflective-simulation
architecturalSections.purposiveDescription: A cross-cutting vertical capability on the right side, reading from every layer and writing in two directions: to the operator (guidance, insight, projections) and to the knowledge graph (derived knowledge as persistent self-knowledge). Maintains trajectories, projections, anomaly detection, option analysis, what-if scenarios, and evaluative assessment imbued with valence. Does not exercise directive control — it offers guidance; the operator decides.
architecturalSections.shortDescription: A cross-cutting meta-knowledge capability reading from all architectural layers, producing guidance and insight for the operator.
architecturalSections.representationalModalitySummary: Mixed — consumes OWL 2 DL, SysML v2, runtime state, and clinical terminologies. Produces natural-language explanations and OWL 2 DL assertions. Internal processing formalism is an open design question.
architecturalSections.persistenceSummary: Derived knowledge persists in the knowledge graph as coordinate space snapshots — named graphs tagged with epistemic status (current, historical, goal, hypothetical, projected). Transient working state does not persist.
architecturalSections.interfacesSummary: Reads from: knowledge graph, instance layers, operational simulation, rules and constraints, terminology. Writes to: operator (guidance) and knowledge graph (derived knowledge). Cross-cutting — not positioned in either stack.
architecturalSections.domainIllustrationSummary: For Paws: answers questions like groomer utilisation trends, what-if for adding Teeth Cleaning, revenue vs goal gap analysis with valence, shampoo consumption anomaly detection, and April revenue projection.

architecturalSections.name: rules-and-constraints
architecturalSections.purposiveDescription: Rules and constraints govern what is permissible in dynamic behaviour — not what structures can exist (that is the ontological layers' job). The green container wraps the bottom two pairs on both stacks. Critical distinction: constraint definitions live in the instance layers above (structural); constraint enforcement happens inside the container at runtime (dynamic). This parallels the governance traceability chain (A8).
architecturalSections.shortDescription: The green container governing what is permissible in dynamic behaviour, wrapping the bottom two pairs on both stacks.
architecturalSections.representationalModalitySummary: Mixed. Definitions: SysML v2 (requirement defs, constraint defs, decision tables). Enforcement: CLP(FD), Temporal guards, XState validation, business rule evaluation. Spans eligibility, scheduling, safety, governance, and probabilistic rule types.
architecturalSections.persistenceSummary: Constraint definitions persist in the model (SysML v2 / knowledge graph). Enforcement results persist as evidence (audit trail, evaluation records).
architecturalSections.interfacesSummary: Inward: governs both business process patterns and operational simulation. Upward: definitions trace to instance layers and regulatory requirements. The reflective simulation reads from this layer to know acceptable operation boundaries.
architecturalSections.domainIllustrationSummary: For Paws: one room per groom at a time (scheduling), groomer must be qualified (capability), correct surcharge order (business rule), second handler for aggressive dogs (safety), current insurance required (compliance).

architecturalSections.name: terminology-and-information-carriers
architecturalSections.purposiveDescription: Semantic grounding for domain-specific terminology and structured information exchange. For clinical tenants: SNOMED CT, openEHR, ICD, FHIR, AQL. For non-clinical tenants: industry-standard codes, service taxonomies, regulatory classification schemes. Distinct from ontological categories (what kinds of things exist) and meta model vocabularies (structural patterns) — this section provides the vocabulary for domain-specific content.
architecturalSections.shortDescription: Semantic grounding for domain-specific terminology and structured information exchange standards.
architecturalSections.representationalModalitySummary: Native formalisms of the standards: SNOMED CT concept hierarchy, openEHR archetypes (ADL), FHIR resource profiles, ICD classification. Imported, not invented.
architecturalSections.persistenceSummary: Terminology servers, CDR instances, FHIR servers — external infrastructure Ontara connects to. Mappings to Ontara's ontological categories persist in the knowledge graph.
architecturalSections.interfacesSummary: The reflective simulation reads terminology for precise explanations. The operational simulation uses it for coded data capture. The mapping ontology bridges internal vocabulary and external standards.
architecturalSections.domainIllustrationSummary: For Paws: thin — possibly breed classification standards. For GSL: dense — SNOMED CT, openEHR archetypes, ICD-11 gender incongruence codes, FHIR for GP communication. Density varies by regulatory tier.

architecturalSections.name: mapping-ontology
architecturalSections.purposiveDescription: The bridge between the two formalisms. Everything above the formalism boundary is OWL 2 DL; everything below is SysML v2. The mapping ontology (B24), itself expressed in OWL, formally declares correspondences: SysML blocks/parts to OWL classes, SysML relationships to OWL object properties, SysML value types to OWL datatype properties. Its existence is committed; its design is deferred.
architecturalSections.shortDescription: The OWL bridge between the two formalisms — formally declaring how SysML v2 elements correspond to ontological classes.
architecturalSections.representationalModalitySummary: OWL 2 DL — the mapping ontology is itself an ontology, living on the OWL side but describing the SysML side. openCAESAR may provide bridge infrastructure.
architecturalSections.persistenceSummary: Triple store (knowledge graph), alongside the domain ontologies and system ontological categories.
architecturalSections.interfacesSummary: Interfaces with everything: connects ontological layers on both stacks, enables SysML content to be represented in and retrieved from the knowledge graph. Makes the knowledge-graph-as-canonical commitment (B22) technically feasible.
architecturalSections.domainIllustrationSummary: For Paws: SysML part def ServiceOffering maps to OWL class ontara:ServiceOffering classified under BFO via OCE. Part usage standardGroom maps to OWL individual paws:StandardGroom. Attribute basePrice maps to datatype property ontara:hasBasePrice.

architecturalSections.name: knowledge-graph
architecturalSections.purposiveDescription: The eventual canonical store for the entire Ontara model (B22). Provides capabilities SysML alone cannot: open-world reasoning, automatic classification, consistency checking against BFO axioms, SPARQL semantic querying, formal TBox/ABox separation mapping to the meta model/instance distinction, and named-graph infrastructure for coordinate space snapshots. Adding a new axis to the coordinate space is adding triples with a new predicate — no schema migration required.
architecturalSections.shortDescription: The OWL 2 DL triple store as the eventual canonical store for the entire Ontara model.
architecturalSections.representationalModalitySummary: OWL 2 DL — the native formalism. Target home for everything above the formalism boundary and, via the mapping ontology, a canonical representation of everything below it.
architecturalSections.persistenceSummary: Triple store / graph database — this is a persistence section. Persists: ontological axioms, meta model vocabulary, instance data, weighted relationships, comprehension metadata, coordinate space snapshots, reflective simulation derived knowledge, mapping ontology.
architecturalSections.interfacesSummary: Everything feeds into or reads from the knowledge graph. SPARQL is the query interface. The SysML v2 model is a projection maintained in bidirectional sync.
architecturalSections.domainIllustrationSummary: For Paws: BFO axioms, OCE ontology, BMM vocabulary as OWL classes, all Paws entities as OWL individuals, weighted relationships, coordinate space snapshots for current state, goals, and what-if scenarios.

architecturalSections.name: sysml-v2
architecturalSections.purposiveDescription: The engineering projection — the view of the canonical model that the architect and developer work with directly. Currently the primary representation; will remain the primary working representation even when the knowledge graph becomes canonical. Holds meta model vocabularies, instances, comprehension metadata, constraint definitions, PatternCatalogue entries, and structural relationships. The entire generation pipeline reads from SysML v2.
architecturalSections.shortDescription: The engineering projection — the view of the canonical model that the architect works with directly in Syside Modeler.
architecturalSections.representationalModalitySummary: SysML v2 — the native formalism. 11 core .sysml files, approximately 73 packages. Target: engineering projection from the knowledge graph, maintained in bidirectional sync via the mapping ontology.
architecturalSections.persistenceSummary: .sysml files in the git repository (model/ and exercises/ directories). Git provides version control.
architecturalSections.interfacesSummary: The generation pipeline reads from SysML v2 and produces JSON, Mermaid, TypeScript, constraint evaluators. The knowledge graph will maintain bidirectional sync. Syside Modeler is the authoring environment.
architecturalSections.domainIllustrationSummary: For Paws: one .sysml file (PawsGroomingDomain.sysml) with part usages instantiating BMM part defs plus 7 StakeholderModel instantiations. Source for gen_model_introspection.py.

architecturalSections.name: openehr
architecturalSections.purposiveDescription: The clinical data architecture for healthcare tenants. openEHR provides archetypes (reusable clinical data building blocks), templates, and a CDR storing archetype-structured clinical data with AQL semantic querying. For clinical tenants like GSL, openEHR is the persistence and data architecture for clinical content. Non-clinical tenants do not use this section — tenant variation made architectural.
architecturalSections.shortDescription: The clinical data architecture for healthcare tenants — archetypes, templates, and a Clinical Data Repository.
architecturalSections.representationalModalitySummary: ADL for archetype definitions, openEHR reference model for data structures, AQL for queries. The coffee shop demonstrator has a working EHRbase integration with three archetypes.
architecturalSections.persistenceSummary: EHRbase CDR — a dedicated clinical data repository, separate from the operational database and knowledge graph. Clinical data has specific regulatory requirements best served by a purpose-built CDR.
architecturalSections.interfacesSummary: The operational simulation interacts with the CDR for clinical data. Terminology layer provides SNOMED CT coding. The reflective simulation reads clinical data within access control bounds. The mapping ontology bridges archetypes and Ontara's ontological model.
architecturalSections.domainIllustrationSummary: For Paws: empty — non-clinical tenant. For GSL: central — archetypes for hormone monitoring, referral compositions, mental health assessments, and the CDR as authoritative clinical record.

architecturalSections.name: temporal
architecturalSections.purposiveDescription: The execution infrastructure for the operational simulation (L5). Temporal provides durable workflow orchestration: sequences of work that survive process restarts, handle retries and timeouts, manage compensation, and maintain explicit state. Temporal is the infrastructure the simulation runs on — not the simulation itself — just as the triple store is the infrastructure the knowledge graph runs on.
architecturalSections.shortDescription: The execution infrastructure for the operational simulation — durable workflow orchestration surviving process restarts.
architecturalSections.representationalModalitySummary: Temporal workflow definitions, activity definitions, state management — execution-level primitives, the most concrete content in the architecture. Generated from the model via the compilation pipeline.
architecturalSections.persistenceSummary: Temporal's own persistence layer (typically PostgreSQL-backed) stores workflow state, execution history, and task queues — operational persistence, durable relative to individual requests.
architecturalSections.interfacesSummary: The operational simulation runs on Temporal. The generation pipeline produces Temporal workflow code. Human actors and connected applications participate as activity executors. System domains are implemented as workers, activities, and child workflows.
architecturalSections.domainIllustrationSummary: For Paws: orchestrates the end-to-end grooming workflow (book through pay and record), scheduling engine, inventory monitoring, and financial processing — each generated from business process patterns with semantic identity preserved.

architecturalSections.name: operator
architecturalSections.purposiveDescription: The human business operator — the guidance target for the entire architecture. Every other section exists to serve the operator's understanding and agency. The reflective simulation produces guidance for the operator. The console presents the model to the operator. Valence (L7) is the operator's declared conception of good performance. Goal states in the coordinate space are the operator's aspirations made formal. The architecture is invisible to the operator; what they see is a system that understands the business.
architecturalSections.shortDescription: The human business operator — the guidance target for the entire architecture; every other section exists to serve their understanding and agency.
architecturalSections.representationalModalitySummary: Not a representational section in the usual sense. The operator's inputs (valence declarations, goals, configuration, instance content) are model content. The system's outputs (explanations, guidance, projections) are the reflective simulation's products rendered for human consumption.
architecturalSections.persistenceSummary: Operator preferences, goal state declarations, and valence definitions persist in the model (knowledge graph / SysML v2). Interaction history may persist for trajectory analysis.
architecturalSections.interfacesSummary: Interacts with the console (navigation, comprehension, relationship graph). The reflective simulation writes guidance. The operator writes business instance content, valence declarations, and goal states. The ultimate audience for A2 (self-describing system).
architecturalSections.domainIllustrationSummary: For Paws: Sam uses the console to understand business structure, see performance against goals, explore what-if scenarios, and receive guidance — without needing to understand SysML, OWL, BFO, or Temporal.

purposiveDescription.description: A distinct service that your business offers — something a customer can choose, pay for, and receive. When you define a service offering, the system connects it to the activities required to deliver it, the resources it consumes, and the price the customer pays.

weightedRelationships.rationale: A service offering is the concrete realisation of a value proposition. A change to what is offered requires reassessing the promise of value it delivers.
Every service offering exists for defined customer segments. A change to what is offered requires reassessing who it is for.
Each offering has a pricing basis. A change to the offering directly affects how it is priced.
Every service offering requires activities to deliver it. A change to the offering requires reassessing the activity types involved.
Channels deliver service offerings to customers. A change to the offering may require reviewing delivery channels, but the coupling is not definitional.
The catalogue records the business decision to offer something. A change to the offering may require updating catalogue entries, but the catalogue is operational, not definitional.
Claims support the value proposition which the offering delivers. A change to the offering may require reviewing claims, but the link is mediated through the value proposition.

Informed consent must be obtained and recorded

elements.doc:
Prescribing must follow an approved clinical protocol.

monitoring schedule is determined by the prescribing
protocol and the patient's clinical stability.

Categorised contraindication status for prescribing
decisions. Simplification of the full clinical

elements.doc:
Status of an individual outcome measurement
against its defined target.
pending: measurement due but not yet taken
measured: data collected, not yet evaluated
targetMet: evaluated and within target
targetNotMet: evaluated and outside target
indeterminate: data insufficient for evaluation

elements.doc:
How often an outcome is measured. Determines
which measurement points include this outcome.

elements.doc:
How a target value is compared against an actual
measurement. Used in OutcomeDefinition to specify
the target condition.

elements.name: row01
elements.doc:
Oestrogen preference, no contraindications,
low baseline — standard transdermal patch.

elements.name: row02

Oestrogen preference, VTE risk —
transdermal preferred over oral to avoid
first-pass hepatic effects. Reduced dose.

elements.name: row03

Oestrogen preference, liver disease —
transdermal to bypass hepatic metabolism.

elements.name: row04

Oestrogen preference, cardiac risk —
transdermal, low starting dose with close
monitoring.

elements.name: row05

requires specialist review. Lowest-risk option
as starting point for discussion.

elements.name: row06

Testosterone preference, no contraindications —
standard IM injection.

elements.name: row07

Testosterone preference, needle aversion or
patient preference for self-administration —
transdermal gel.

elements.name: row08
elements.doc:
Testosterone preference, cardiac risk —
gel preferred over injection for more stable
serum levels. Reduced starting dose.

elements.name: row09

transdermal to avoid hepatic first-pass.

hepatically metabolised at standard doses).

elements.name: row01
elements.doc:
Normal hormones, 12+ weeks, no significant
side effects, patient satisfied — stable.
Continue current regimen, standard monitoring.

elements.name: row02
elements.doc:
Normal hormones, 12+ weeks, no significant
side effects, patient neutral — stable but
explore satisfaction concerns. Continue
regimen with reduced monitoring interval.

elements.name: row03
elements.doc:
Normal hormones but less than 12 weeks on
treatment — too early to declare stable.
Continue and recheck.

elements.name: row04
elements.doc:
Low hormone levels — dose likely insufficient.
Adjust dose upward.

elements.name: row05
elements.doc:
High hormone levels — dose may need reducing.
Adjust dose downward.

elements.name: row06
elements.doc:
Normal hormones but warning-level side effects —
may need route or formulation change.
Increase monitoring, clinical review.

elements.name: row07
elements.doc:
Critical side effects regardless of hormone
levels — urgent clinical review.

elements.name: row08
elements.doc:
Suppressed hormone levels — possible over-
suppression. Urgent review to assess dose
and clinical status.

maturity level. Each domain instantiation is separate
so maturity can vary per domain.

elements.name: separationOfRepresentationAndExecution
elements.doc:
The foundational architectural commitment: knowledge
lives in the representation layer (SysML model),
execution is derived from it.

attributes.name: description
attributes.value: Knowledge lives in the representation layer (SysML model). Execution is derived from it via generation or configuration. The model is the source of truth

elements.name: selfDescribingSystem
elements.doc:
The system knows what it is, what it should be,
and what the gap is. Self-knowledge is structural,
not bolt-on.

attributes.name: description
attributes.value: The system carries knowledge about itself: what it is (OperationalStateAggregator), what it should be (GoalProjector), and what the gap is (GapAnalyser). Self-knowledge is structural, not bolted on.

elements.name: modelGeneratesEverything
elements.doc:
Corollary of separation: SysML as single source
of truth. Generators emit TypeScript, XState,
Temporal, Mermaid, and more.

attributes.value: Practical corollary of separation: the SysML model generates TypeScript types, XState machines, Temporal workflows, Mermaid diagrams, and more. Changes to the model propagate to the running system.

elements.name: twoMetaModelDistinction
elements.doc:
Business meta model (what the business is) and
system meta model (how the system works)
are distinct and independently iterable.

attributes.name: description
attributes.value: Business meta model (what the business is and offers) and business system meta model (how the system is structured and operates) are distinct. Each can iterate independently. Per gsl-architecture-clarification-two-meta-models.

elements.name: coffeeshopFirst

architectural capability gets a CSW equivalent first.

elements.name: deterministicOverProbabilistic
elements.doc:
Clinical decisions use deterministic, inspectable,
auditable logic — not probabilistic LLM inference.

attributes.name: description
attributes.value: Clinical decision support uses deterministic, inspectable, auditable logic (constraint evaluation, decision tables, Prolog rules). Probabilistic LLM inference is not acceptable for safety-critical clinical reasoning.

elements.name: patientAutonomy
elements.doc:
The generational self-service roadmap supports
increasing patient autonomy and informed choice.

attributes.name: description
attributes.value: The system supports a generational roadmap from clinician-gated (Gen 1) to patient-initiated (Gen 3) self-service. Patient autonomy is a design goal, not an afterthought. Informed choice requires the system to explain its reasoning.

elements.name: clinicalGovernanceAsFirstClass
elements.doc:
Auditability is structural, not bolted on. Clinical
governance is a first-class system concern.

attributes.value: Auditability is structural, not bolted on. The domain layer exists specifically to be auditable for clinical governance. Audit trails, provenance tracking, and governance dashboards are architectural commitments, not features.

elements.name: fourLayerItemModel

external references. Separates intrinsic properties
from business decisions from operational state from
external knowledge.

generation. The model is the source; generators
